claims.claim: B26 lab: LoRA with r 4 and alpha 8 on queries and values plus a new head trained 1,123 of 26,979 values; mean validation accuracy over seeds 0 to 2 was 0.967 (0.990, 0.982, 0.929) on 60 labels against 0.992 for full fine-tuning, and 0.995 against 0.998 on 600 labels.

concept_html:
Full fine-tuning changes every weight and stores a full copy per task. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes a layer's weight W, shape (d_out, d_in), and learns a small change made of two matrices: A, shape (r, d_in), and B, shape (d_out, r), with a small rank r:

y = x @ W.T + (alpha / r) * (x @ A.T @ B.T)

The product B @ A has the shape of W but at most rank r. alpha / r scales the update, so you can change r without retuning the learning rate.

  • Few values to train. A 768 by 768 layer holds 589,824 weights. With r = 8, A and B hold 8 * (768 + 768) = 12,288, about 2%.
  • B starts at zero. A starts random and B at zero, so B @ A is zero and the adapted model starts identical to the pretrained one. peft 0.21 does this by default.
  • Merge for prediction. After training, fold the update in: W_merged = W + (alpha / r) * B @ A. The merged layer is an ordinary linear layer with no extra cost. Keep A and B apart instead, and one frozen base model serves many tasks, each with its own small adapter.
  • Where to put it. A common choice is the attention query and value projections.

In the B26 lab, LoRA with r = 4 on queries and values, plus a new head, trained 1,123 of 26,979 values. On 60 labels it reached 0.967 mean accuracy over three seeds, against 0.992 for full fine-tuning. Its seeds also spread wider, from 0.929 to 0.990. On 600 labels the gap closed to 0.995 against 0.998.

LoRA does not make the forward pass cheaper during training: the frozen weight still runs. It saves the memory for gradients and optimiser state of the frozen weights, and the storage of one full model copy per task.

lines: import numpy as np
def lora_init(d_in: int, d_out: int, r: int, seed: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
"""A random, B zero, so the update starts at zero.
Raises:
ValueError: If r is below 1 or larger than d_in or d_out.
"""
if not 1 <= r <= min(d_in, d_out):
raise ValueError(f"r must be in 1..{min(d_in, d_out)}, got {r}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
return rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(d_in), size=(r, d_in)), np.zeros((d_out, r))
def lora_forward(x: np.ndarray, W: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, B: np.ndarray, alpha: float) -> np.ndarray:
"""Frozen layer plus the scaled low-rank update, for x of shape (n, d_in)."""
r = A.shape[0]
return x @ W.T + (alpha / r) * (x @ A.T @ B.T)
def merge_lora(W: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, B: np.ndarray, alpha: float) -> np.ndarray:
"""One weight matrix equal to the frozen layer plus its update."""
return W + (alpha / A.shape[0]) * B @ A

notes.html: A random and B zero: B @ A starts at zero, so the model starts as pretrained.
x @ A.T @ B.T never builds the d_out by d_in product, only (n, r) then (n, d_out).
Merging uses the same alpha / r scale, so merged and unmerged outputs match.

exercises.solution:
import numpy as np


def lora_forward(x: np.ndarray, W: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, B: np.ndarray, alpha: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Frozen layer plus the scaled low-rank update.

    Args:
        x: Inputs, shape (n, d_in).
        W: Frozen weight, shape (d_out, d_in).
        A: Down projection, shape (r, d_in).
        B: Up projection, shape (d_out, r).
        alpha: Scale numerator; the update is multiplied by alpha / r.

    Returns:
        Outputs, shape (n, d_out).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If A's width differs from W's or B is not (d_out, r).
    """
    r = A.shape[0]
    if A.shape[1] != W.shape[1] or B.shape != (W.shape[0], r):
        raise ValueError(f"shapes do not fit: W {W.shape}, A {A.shape}, B {B.shape}")
    return x @ W.T + (alpha / r) * (x @ A.T @ B.T)

def lora_forward(x: np.ndarray, W: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, B: np.ndarray, alpha: float) -> np.ndarray:
"""Frozen layer plus the scaled low-rank update.
Args:
x: Inputs, shape (n, d_in).
W: Frozen weight, shape (d_out, d_in).
A: Down projection, shape (r, d_in).
B: Up projection, shape (d_out, r).
alpha: Scale numerator; the update is multiplied by alpha / r.
Returns:
Outputs, shape (n, d_out).
Raises:
ValueError: If A's width differs from W's or B is not (d_out, r).
"""
r = A.shape[0]
if A.shape[1] != W.shape[1] or B.shape != (W.shape[0], r):
raise ValueError(f"shapes do not fit: W {W.shape}, A {A.shape}, B {B.shape}")
return x @ W.T + (alpha / r) * (x @ A.T @ B.T)

title: LoRA, fine-tuning with a low-rank update
why_html: A team fine-tuned one text encoder for each of 12 survey clients, each a full copy of 110 million weights. Storage and loading time grew with every client. Switching to LoRA adapters kept one frozen base model and 12 small adapter files, and each client's accuracy stayed within a point of its fully fine-tuned model.
